properties.title: Medical world models: representing medical states, modelling clinical dynamics and guiding intervention policies
Medical world models: representing medical states, modelling clinical dynamics and guiding intervention policies

properties.name: Three functional streams
properties.content: Transition-ready state representation; future clinical trajectories; intervention comparison, sequential optimization and embodied control. Taxonomy, not evaluated capabilities of the review.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Four future-state domains
properties.content: Care/event, imaging, biological/mechanistic and procedural futures have different states, clocks, action meanings and validity constraints.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Composition blueprint
properties.content: Serial pipeline: explicit intermodule outputs without shared gradients; shared-state: multiple functions reuse a common state; closed-loop: perception, action-conditioned simulation and decisions feed back. Disease-level end-to-end reliability is an open requirement.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Observation and state contract
properties.content: Observations are partial noisy irregular records; persistent patient state is distinct from an observation. Action-conditioned futures need explicit clinical action semantics; observational prediction alone is not causal treatment identification.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

BOX 1
What is a world model?
World models are internal models that learn how an environment evolves and
how actions change future states [7–10]. At their core, they can be defined
as action-conditioned transition models over states,p(s t+1 |s t, at), wheres t
denotes the current state anda t denotes an action. The state need not be a raw
observation. It can be a compact latent representation that preserves informa-
tion needed for future prediction and control. Modern neural world models often
organize this core around observationso t, latent statess t, actionsa t, a transi-
tion or dynamics modelp(s t+1 |s t, at) and, when the model is used for planning
or training, an objective or cost function that scores future states or prediction
errors [7–10].
World models are useful when an agent must imagine possible futures before
acting. In autonomous driving, a model can roll out how a traffic scene may
evolve under candidate manoeuvres. In robotics, it can predict how pushing,
grasping or navigation actions may change object configurations, contacts and
goals [11–13]. In spatial intelligence, video generation, games and interactive
environments, related models infer 3D structure, learn action-controllable worlds
or support planning inside learned latent environments [8–10, 14].
World models differ from adjacent technologies by their functional role. Foun-
dation models provide reusable representations, but may not support rollouts.
Generative models synthesize plausible samples, but realism alone does not imply
action-conditioned dynamics. Digital twins emphasize high-fidelity replicas of
specific systems, whereas world models can be learned, latent and task-oriented.
Causal models estimate interventions and counterfactuals, but may not provide
long-horizon simulated trajectories. Model-free policies choose actions without
necessarily exposing an inspectable model of future states.

because the functions are inspectable: one can ask what state was used, what future
was generated and how the future was scored. Its limitation is that the modules may
still be optimized separately, so errors in state estimation or rollout can be handed
downstream to the decision module.

Closed-loop composition turns these issues into a system-level problem. Many cur-
rent systems combine a state encoder, a trajectory generator and a decision head,
but do not yet show that the full perception–dynamics–planning loop remains reli-
able when embedded in clinical workflows. A clinically useful simulator should make
its state assumptions explicit, communicate uncertainty, expose alternative futures for
inspection and support human oversight rather than opaque automation. The next
stage is not merely to build larger medical generative models, but to build clinically
testable simulators whose states are sufficient, transitions are intervention-sensitive,
futures are uncertain but calibrated and recommendations remain inspectable by
clinicians [16, 84, 85].
7.2 Data, F AIR infrastructure and evaluation
The remaining challenges are infrastructural. The limiting resource for medical world
models is not simply the number of patients, but the availability of records that con-
nect a current state, an intervention or action, a time interval and a subsequent state.

Appendix A Key concepts in medical world models
Box 2 — Key concepts in medical world models.
ObservationA measurement or record available to the model, such as images, EHR events,
laboratory values, physiological signals, reports, molecular data or procedural video. Obser-
vations are often partial, noisy and irregularly sampled, and are used to infer patient
state.
Patient stateA compact representation of the current patient, inferred from observations
such as images, EHRs, physiological signals, reports, molecular data or multimodal records.
A useful state should preserve information needed for future transitions, not only for static
prediction.
Policy, intervention or actionA decision variable or concrete input that can alter future
states. In medicine this includes treatment policies, doses, procedures, monitoring decisions,
follow-up strategies, molecular perturbations, probe movements, robotic commands or the
choice to withhold treatment.
Transition or dynamics modelA model of how patient states evolve over time, commonly
written asp(s t+1 |s t, at) when transitions are action-conditioned. Dynamics may be learned
from data, specified by mechanisms or built as a hybrid.
RolloutA simulated sequence of future states generated by repeatedly applying a transition
model. Rollouts can expose possible trajectories, but they also accumulate uncertainty and
model error.
Objective or costA criterion used to train predictions or judge future states, actions or trajec-
tories. In medicine, this may reflect survival, safety, treatment response, functional outcome,
complication avoidance, information gain or procedural success. In reinforcement-learning
settings, it may be implemented as a reward.
Counterfactual trajectoryA possible future under an alternative action or treatment path.
Counterfactual trajectories are central to decision-making but require causal assumptions
beyond ordinary forecasting.
